title: Hubble Interacting Galaxy UGC 9618
caption: Interacting galaxy pair UGC 9618 (Arp 302), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 9618, VV 340, Arp 302, VV 340A, VV 340B, KPG 446B · constellation Boötes · about 450 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration, and A. Evans (University of Virginia, Charlottesville/NRAO/Stony Brook University)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Two spiral galaxies sit side by side at very different angles. On the left, VV 340A is seen edge-on, while VV 340B on the right is seen face-on. The pair is cataloged as UGC 9618, VV 340 and Arp 302, the last being the 302nd entry in Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.

Both galaxies are very rich in gas, and their interaction is still at an early stage. Even so, massive stars are already being born as quickly as in the busiest giant star-forming regions of our own Milky Way. The gas around those young stars radiates an enormous amount of infrared light.

The pair lies 450 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Boötes. The image is part of NASA's April 2008 collection of 59 interacting and merging galaxies. NASA notes that galaxy collisions like this unfold over several hundred million years.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys used a blue filter, F435W (B), and a near-infrared filter, F814W (I). NASA shows F435W in blue, F814W in red, and a blend of both in green.
understand.eye: The strong infrared glow from the pair's star-forming gas is invisible to the eye, and even the near-infrared filter used here records light beyond human vision.

explore: Most of the anniversary images, according to NASA, came from GOALS, the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey. It brings together Hubble pictures with data from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope, Chandra X-ray Observatory and Galaxy Evolution Explorer to study galaxies that shine brightly in infrared light.
